y-m-70-01.title: Where did the solution for a point on a parabola go wrong?
y-m-70-01.topic: Conic sections: the definition of a parabola (focus, directrix) and distance
y-m-70-01.goal: Find the line with an error in a solution that uses the definition of a parabola (the distance to the focus equals the distance to the directrix), check the answer in a way that does not repeat the same error, and test the corrected relationship with specific points.
y-m-70-01.material: This problem asks for all the points P on the parabola y²=12x for which the distance PF from the focus F to P is 9. (Coordinate plane; the unit of length is omitted. y² is read 'y squared'.) Minjae's solution appears at the first step.
y-m-70-01.thinking.0: Checking the logic between the lines of a solution
y-m-70-01.thinking.1: Choosing an independent check that does not repeat the error
y-m-70-01.thinking.2: Testing the corrected relationship with specific cases
y-m-70-01.prereq.0: Assume the learner is taking the high-school 'Geometry' elective course. 'H2' is only a difficulty and support level for this production assignment; it does not mean the Ministry of Education assigns this course to a particular grade.
y-m-70-01.prereq.1: The focus (p, 0) and directrix x=−p of the parabola y²=4px, and the definition of a parabola
y-m-70-01.prereq.2: Distance between two points on the coordinate plane
y-m-70-01.s.s1.prompt: Choose the first line in Minjae's solution that is wrong.
y-m-70-01.s.s1.hint.0: Check, one line at a time, whether each line really follows from the line right before it.
y-m-70-01.s.s1.hint.1: Mark −3 and the point x=1 on a number line and count the distance between them directly, then compare it with the value you get by putting x=1 into the expression in line 3.
y-m-70-01.s.s1.line.0: y²=12x is the parabola y²=4px with p=3, so the focus is F(3, 0) and the directrix is x=−3.
y-m-70-01.s.s1.line.1: For a point P(x, y) on the parabola, the distance PF from P to the focus equals the distance from P to the directrix.
y-m-70-01.s.s1.line.2: The distance from P to the directrix x=−3 is x−3.
y-m-70-01.s.s1.line.3: PF=9, so x−3=9, that is, x=12.
y-m-70-01.s.s1.explain: Line 3 went wrong. The directrix is x=−3 and the points on the parabola have x≥0, so P is to the right of the directrix. So the distance between P and the directrix is not x−3 but x−(−3)=x+3. Correcting it gives x+3=9, x=6, y²=72, so P(6, 6√2) or P(6, −6√2). Lines 4 and 5 are results that inherited the error of line 3.
y-m-70-01.s.s2.prompt: What is the most useful way to confirm that Minjae's answer P(12, 12) is not an answer to the problem?
y-m-70-01.s.s2.hint.0: A check means putting the answer into 'the condition the problem requires', not into 'what the solution produced'. What was the condition of the problem?
y-m-70-01.s.s2.hint.1: Write what value you get when you compute that condition directly with P(12, 12).
y-m-70-01.s.s2.o.a: Follow and write out Minjae's solution once more from the start to see whether the same answer comes out
y-m-70-01.s.s2.r.a: Repeating the same solution repeats the same error. It is not a check independent of the solution.
y-m-70-01.s.s2.o.b: Substitute the point P(12, 12) found to see whether it satisfies y²=12x
y-m-70-01.s.s2.r.b: P(12, 12) really is a point on the parabola. This check shows that it does not test the part with the error (the distance condition).
y-m-70-01.s.s2.o.c: Calculate the distance between P(12, 12) and F(3, 0) and see whether it is 9
y-m-70-01.s.s2.r.c: This idea tests the condition the problem required directly and separately from the solution.
y-m-70-01.s.s2.o.d: Since the answer came out neatly with integer coordinates, think it is probably right
y-m-70-01.s.s2.r.d: Neatness is not evidence of correctness. It does not check whether the answer satisfies the required condition.
y-m-70-01.s.s2.explain: The distance between P(12, 12) and F(3, 0) is √(9²+12²)=√225=15, which is not 9. Whether P is on the parabola is passed even by the answer of a wrong solution, so it cannot catch the error. Calculating the condition the problem requires (PF=9) directly and separately from the solution is the independent check.
y-m-70-01.s.s3.prompt: Let's test whether the corrected relationship 'PF = x+3' is right. Find 2 points P(x, y) on the parabola y²=12x where x and y are both integers, with different values of x, and for each point calculate and write the distance d to F(3, 0) directly with the distance formula between two points.
y-m-70-01.s.s3.hint.0: In y²=12x, find values of x like x=3, 12, 27 for which 12x is a perfect square, and find y.
y-m-70-01.s.s3.hint.1: Square the differences of the coordinates of the point you found and F(3, 0), add them, take the square root, and compare with x+3.
y-m-70-01.s.s3.fail.c1: x and y are not integers.
y-m-70-01.s.s3.ok.c2: The point is on the parabola y²=12x.
y-m-70-01.s.s3.fail.c2: The point is not on the parabola. Check whether y squared equals 12x.
y-m-70-01.s.s3.ok.c3: d equals the distance to F.
y-m-70-01.s.s3.fail.c3: d differs from the distance between P and F(3, 0). Calculate (x−3)²+y².
y-m-70-01.s.s3.explain: For example, at (3, 6), d=6=3+3; at (12, 12), d=15=12+3; at (27, 18), d=30=27+3. At every point PF=x+3 is confirmed. So PF=9 happens only at x=6, and then y²=72, so the answers of this problem are not points with integer coordinates.

y-m-70-02.title: Can we know the distance from a point on an ellipse to the other focus?
y-m-70-02.topic: Conic sections: the definition of an ellipse (the sum of distances to the two foci)
y-m-70-02.goal: Learn that the distance from one point on an ellipse to one focus alone cannot fix the distance to the other focus, say what else is needed, and judge the range of possible distances when the equation is given.
y-m-70-02.material: Let F and F′ be the two foci of an ellipse, and let P be a point on this ellipse. Only PF=7 is known, and you want to find PF′. (All lengths are in the same unit. x²/25 is read 'x squared over 25'.)
y-m-70-02.thinking.0: Judging whether the information is enough
y-m-70-02.thinking.1: Naming the information that is needed
y-m-70-02.thinking.2: Reasoning about the range of possible values
y-m-70-02.prereq.0: Assume the learner is taking the high-school 'Geometry' elective course. 'H2' is only a difficulty and support level for this production assignment; it does not mean the Ministry of Education assigns this course to a particular grade.
y-m-70-02.prereq.1: The definition of an ellipse (the sum of the distances to the two foci is constant)
y-m-70-02.prereq.2: The foci of the ellipse x²/a²+y²/b²=1 (a>b>0) are (±c, 0), and c²=a²−b²
y-m-70-02.s.s1.prompt: To fix PF′ as a single value, what else is needed besides what is known now?
y-m-70-02.s.s1.hint.0: Write in words what the 'constant value' in the definition of an ellipse is.
y-m-70-02.s.s1.hint.1: Keep PF=7 and think about an ellipse where the sum is 12 and one where the sum is 20, and compare what PF′ would be in each.
y-m-70-02.s.s1.o.a: The distance FF′ between the two foci (only this value is added)
y-m-70-02.s.s1.r.a: Even knowing only the distance between the foci does not fix what the sum of distances is. Even with the same foci there are many ellipses of different sizes.
y-m-70-02.s.s1.o.b: The y-coordinate of point P (only this value is added)
y-m-70-02.s.s1.r.b: One coordinate of P alone cannot tell the position of the foci or the size of the ellipse. There is not enough to calculate PF′.
y-m-70-02.s.s1.o.c: The length of the major axis of the ellipse (or the equation of the ellipse)
y-m-70-02.s.s1.r.c: This is the value that tells what the sum of the distances to the two foci is fixed at for this ellipse.
y-m-70-02.s.s1.o.d: Nothing more is needed. PF′ is also 7
y-m-70-02.s.s1.r.d: You do not know which point it is, yet you decided it is the same distance from both foci. Where would P have to be for PF=PF′?
y-m-70-02.s.s1.explain: PF+PF′ is the same value (the length of the major axis) at any point on the ellipse. If you do not know that value, PF=7 alone does not fix PF′. FF′ or one coordinate of P alone also does not fix the sum, and setting PF′=PF is right only when P is on the perpendicular line through the middle of the two foci.
y-m-70-02.s.s2.prompt: Now the ellipse x²/25 + y²/9 = 1 is given. The foci are F(4, 0) and F′(−4, 0). (Semi-major axis 5, semi-minor axis 3, 4²=5²−3²) At which points P of this ellipse can PF=7 happen?
y-m-70-02.s.s2.hint.0: Calculate PF at the right vertex (5, 0) and the left vertex (−5, 0) to find the smallest and the largest value of PF.
y-m-70-02.s.s2.hint.1: Check whether 7 is within that range, then find PF′ using the sum of the distances.
y-m-70-02.s.s2.r.a: This solution treated the point as equally far from both foci. For such a point, PF=PF′=5 would be needed.
y-m-70-02.s.s2.r.b: This judgment used the length of the major axis as the sum of the distances.
y-m-70-02.s.s2.o.c: Impossible. PF cannot exceed the semi-major axis 5
y-m-70-02.s.s2.r.c: The semi-major axis is the distance from the center to a vertex. It is a different quantity from the distance from a focus to a point on the ellipse.
y-m-70-02.s.s2.r.d: It looks as if you set the length 10 of the major axis equal to the difference of the two distances, not the sum.
y-m-70-02.s.s2.explain: The length of the major axis is 10, so PF+PF′=10. PF is 5−4=1 at the nearest vertex and 5+4=9 at the farthest vertex, so it can take every value between 1 and 9. 7 is within that range, and then PF′=10−7=3.
y-m-70-02.s.s3.prompt: On the same ellipse, make 3 ordered pairs (p, q) for which there really is a point P with PF=p and PF′=q. (Swapping p and q counts as the same example. You may use decimals.)
y-m-70-02.s.s3.hint.0: First write what p+q must be, then check whether choosing one p fixes q.
y-m-70-02.s.s3.hint.1: Try p less than 1 or greater than 9 and think about whether such a point can really be on the ellipse.
y-m-70-02.s.s3.ok.c1: The sum of the two distances is 10, the length of the major axis.
y-m-70-02.s.s3.fail.c1: p+q is not 10. What was the sum of the distances to the two foci of this ellipse?
y-m-70-02.s.s3.ok.c2: It is within the range of distances a point on the ellipse can have.
y-m-70-02.s.s3.fail.c2: The distance from a point on the ellipse to a focus cannot be less than 1. Recall the distance at the nearest vertex.
y-m-70-02.s.s3.explain: p+q=10, and the value of PF goes from 1 (nearest vertex) to 9 (farthest vertex), so p and q must both be at least 1. All ordered pairs with p between 1 and 9, such as (3, 7), (5, 5) and (1, 9), are possible.

y-m-70-03.title: Does a line with the same slope as an asymptote never meet the hyperbola?
y-m-70-03.topic: Conic sections: positions of a hyperbola's asymptotes and a line
y-m-70-03.goal: Test a generalization built from substituting one asymptote against more lines and revise your judgment, then use the result to build examples of lines with the same slope yourself.
y-m-70-03.material: The asymptotes of the hyperbola H: x²/4 − y²/9 = 1 (read: x squared over 4 minus y squared over 9 equals 1) are y=(3/2)x and y=−(3/2)x. Soyoung said: “A line with the same slope as an asymptote never meets H. An asymptote only gets closer and closer to H without touching it.” Let's evaluate Soyoung's statement by looking at the materials below one at a time.
y-m-70-03.thinking.0: Judging a generalization from partial evidence
y-m-70-03.thinking.1: Revising your judgment and confidence with new evidence
y-m-70-03.thinking.2: Constructing examples of lines that satisfy a condition
y-m-70-03.prereq.0: Assume the learner is taking the high-school 'Geometry' elective course. 'H2' is only a difficulty and support level for this production assignment; it does not mean the Ministry of Education assigns this course to a particular grade.
y-m-70-03.prereq.1: The asymptotes y=±(b/a)x of the hyperbola x²/a²−y²/b²=1
y-m-70-03.prereq.2: Substituting the equation of a line into the equation of a hyperbola and simplifying
y-m-70-03.s.s1.prompt: Looking at the materials one step at a time, choose your current judgment about Soyoung's statement.
y-m-70-03.s.s1.hint.0: Tell apart whether all that has been confirmed so far is 'the asymptote itself' or all lines with the same slope.
y-m-70-03.s.s1.hint.1: Think about what happens if you directly substitute one line that has the same slope but is not an asymptote, such as y=(3/2)x+1.
y-m-70-03.s.s1.st.0.info: Substituting the asymptote y=(3/2)x into the equation of H gives x²/4 − ((3/2)x)²/9 = x²/4 − x²/4 = 0, which is 0 whatever x is. It cannot be 1, so the asymptote does not meet H.
y-m-70-03.s.s1.st.0.ask: Having seen this material, what is your judgment about Soyoung's statement (every line with the same slope never meets H)?
y-m-70-03.s.s1.st.0.after: It has been confirmed that the asymptote itself does not meet H. But Soyoung's statement is about all lines with the same slope, so other lines have not been tested yet.
y-m-70-03.s.s1.st.0.o.a: I think it is right, but only one asymptote has been checked, so my confidence is weak
y-m-70-03.s.s1.st.0.r.a: You confirmed that the asymptote itself does not meet H. You have not yet tested other lines with the same slope.
y-m-70-03.s.s1.st.0.o.b: It is too early to judge. Other lines with the same slope must be tested too
y-m-70-03.s.s1.st.0.r.b: The statement is about 'all lines with the same slope'. You know that the line seen so far is only one of them.
y-m-70-03.s.s1.st.0.o.c: It is wrong. Every line with the same slope meets H
y-m-70-03.s.s1.st.0.r.c: This does not agree with the material that the asymptote does not meet it. It is a judgment declared in the opposite direction without evidence.
y-m-70-03.s.s1.st.1.info: Substituting the line y=(3/2)x+1, which has the same slope, into the equation of H gives x²/4 − ((3/2)x+1)²/9 = −x/3 − 1/9 = 1. So x=−10/3, y=(3/2)(−10/3)+1=−4, and it meets H at the point (−10/3, −4). (Check: (100/9)/4 − 16/9 = 25/9 − 16/9 = 1)
y-m-70-03.s.s1.st.1.ask: Having seen this new material, what is your judgment about Soyoung's statement?
y-m-70-03.s.s1.st.1.after: The point (−10/3, −4) satisfies both the equation of H and the equation of the line, so it is a counterexample. One counterexample makes Soyoung's generalization false.
y-m-70-03.s.s1.st.1.o.a: The calculation must be wrong. If the slope is the same as an asymptote, they cannot meet
y-m-70-03.s.s1.st.1.r.a: This is a judgment that tries to keep the first belief without doing the check calculation (whether the point satisfies the equation of H) yourself.
y-m-70-03.s.s1.st.1.o.b: This line cannot be a counterexample because it does not have the same slope as the asymptote
y-m-70-03.s.s1.st.1.r.b: The slope of y=(3/2)x+1 is 3/2, the same as the asymptote. Check again the condition for being a counterexample.
y-m-70-03.s.s1.st.1.o.c: Soyoung's statement is false. There is a line with the same slope that meets H
y-m-70-03.s.s1.st.1.r.c: This is a judgment that one counterexample broke 'if the slope is the same, it never meets'.
y-m-70-03.s.s1.st.2.info: In general, substituting y=(3/2)x+k gives −(k/3)x − k²/9 = 1, which is a linear equation in x. If k=0 they do not meet; if k≠0, x=−(k²+9)/(3k) is fixed as one value, so they meet at exactly one point.
y-m-70-03.s.s1.st.2.ask: How would you correct Soyoung's statement into a correct sentence?
y-m-70-03.s.s1.st.2.after: Both b and d are true. b even tells which line falls in which case (k=0 or k≠0), while d only states the possible results.
y-m-70-03.s.s1.st.2.o.a: A line with the same slope always meets H at two points
y-m-70-03.s.s1.st.2.r.a: For two points to appear, the substituted equation must be a quadratic equation. In the material above, the equation was linear.
y-m-70-03.s.s1.st.2.o.b: Among lines with the same slope, only the asymptote itself does not meet H, and the rest meet it at one point
y-m-70-03.s.s1.st.2.r.b: You explained all the cases by dividing into k=0 and k≠0.
y-m-70-03.s.s1.st.2.o.c: Soyoung is right. The counterexample came from a calculation error
y-m-70-03.s.s1.st.2.r.c: You treated a result checked in two steps as an error.
y-m-70-03.s.s1.st.2.o.d: A line with the same slope either does not meet H or meets it at one point (never two points)
y-m-70-03.s.s1.st.2.r.d: This is a true sentence that covers all cases. It does not say which case goes which way.
y-m-70-03.s.s1.reflect: At first you could believe 'none of them meet' from one asymptote, but a generalization is hard to be sure of from a single case. In the next material, when one line with the same slope met H, the generalization broke, and the last material showed exactly 'when they do not meet'. Say which part of the materials was the reason you changed your judgment.
y-m-70-03.s.s2.prompt: Choose a point P(x, y) on the hyperbola H: x²/4 − y²/9 = 1, and find and write the y-intercept k of the line y=(3/2)x+k with slope 3/2 passing through P. k must not be 0, and make 3 examples with different k. (You may write decimals; an error within 0.05 is accepted.)
y-m-70-03.s.s2.hint.0: Find points that satisfy 9x²−4y²=36. What is x when y=0? What about when x=2.5?
y-m-70-03.s.s2.hint.1: After choosing a point, put its coordinates into y=(3/2)x+k to find k.
y-m-70-03.s.s2.ok.c1: The point is on the hyperbola.
y-m-70-03.s.s2.fail.c1: The point is not on the hyperbola. Calculate whether x²/4−y²/9 equals 1.
y-m-70-03.s.s2.ok.c2: The line passes through P and has slope 3/2.
y-m-70-03.s.s2.fail.c2: With that k, the line y=(3/2)x+k does not pass through P. Put in the coordinates of P and find k again.
y-m-70-03.s.s2.ok.c3: k is not 0 (the line is not an asymptote).
y-m-70-03.s.s2.fail.c3: k is 0 or too small. The line must not be an asymptote.
y-m-70-03.s.s2.explain: For example, if P(2, 0), then k=0−3=−3; if P(5/2, 9/4), then k=9/4−15/4=−3/2; if P(−5/2, −9/4), then k=3/2. Even though these lines have the same slope as an asymptote, each meets H at the one point P.

y-m-70-04.title: If the dot products are equal, are the two vectors equal too?
y-m-70-04.topic: Plane vectors: properties of the dot product and counterexamples
y-m-70-04.goal: Test with a counterexample whether the cancelling rule that holds for numbers ('if ab=ac and a≠0 then b=c') also holds for the dot product of vectors, and pick out the conditions that make it hold.
y-m-70-04.material: For numbers, if a≠0 and ab=ac, then b=c. Jeonghyeok thought vectors work the same way and said: “When a=(2, 1), if a·b=a·c then b=c.” (a·b is the dot product of a and b, that is, the value you get by multiplying the components and adding. All vectors are on the coordinate plane.)
y-m-70-04.thinking.0: Doubting whether a rule for numbers can be moved to other objects
y-m-70-04.thinking.1: Building a counterexample that satisfies the conditions yourself
y-m-70-04.thinking.2: Testing whether extra conditions are enough
y-m-70-04.prereq.0: Assume the learner is taking the high-school 'Geometry' elective course. 'H2' is only a difficulty and support level for this production assignment; it does not mean the Ministry of Education assigns this course to a particular grade.
y-m-70-04.prereq.1: Component form of plane vectors and the dot product a·b=a₁b₁+a₂b₂
y-m-70-04.prereq.2: Properties of the dot product when two vectors are parallel or perpendicular
y-m-70-04.s.s1.prompt: To find out whether Jeonghyeok's statement always holds, which (b, c) would be most useful to test?
y-m-70-04.s.s1.hint.0: When a claim has the form 'if condition then conclusion', what must an example that breaks the claim satisfy and what must it violate, the condition or the conclusion?
y-m-70-04.s.s1.hint.1: First choose one vector whose dot product with a=(2, 1) is known, then change its components and look for another vector whose dot product stays the same.
y-m-70-04.s.s1.o.a: Test many pairs where b and c are the same vector
y-m-70-04.s.s1.r.a: If b=c, then a·b=a·c always holds. These are not pairs that can break the claim.
y-m-70-04.s.s1.o.b: Test only vectors that have the same direction as a
y-m-70-04.s.s1.r.b: You are testing only a special case. Even if it holds there, you cannot know about other cases.
y-m-70-04.s.s1.o.c: Test vectors that are very large
y-m-70-04.s.s1.r.c: The size has nothing directly to do with whether this claim holds.
y-m-70-04.s.s1.o.d: Look for pairs with a·b=a·c and b≠c
y-m-70-04.s.s1.r.d: Since the claim says 'always', this idea looks for a pair that satisfies the condition but goes against the conclusion.
y-m-70-04.s.s1.explain: A claim of 'always' is broken by a single pair that satisfies the condition (a·b=a·c) while going against the conclusion (b=c). So the most useful thing is to look for such a pair yourself.
y-m-70-04.s.s2.prompt: For a=(2, 1), make 2 pairs of vectors b=(b₁, b₂), c=(c₁, c₂) with a·b=a·c but b≠c. The two pairs must have different b−c (swapping b and c, or changing only the sign of b−c, counts as the same example).
y-m-70-04.s.s2.hint.0: First choose one b and calculate a·b.
y-m-70-04.s.s2.hint.1: See how much a·c changes when you change one component of c, then change the other component suitably to bring the dot product back.
y-m-70-04.s.s2.fail.c1: Calculate a·b=2b₁+b₂ and a·c=2c₁+c₂ separately. The two values are not equal.
y-m-70-04.s.s2.ok.c2: b and c are different vectors.
y-m-70-04.s.s2.fail.c2: b and c are the same vector. They must be different to be a counterexample.
y-m-70-04.s.s2.explain: Example: if b=(1, 3), c=(2, 1), then a·b=2+3=5 and a·c=4+1=5 are equal but b≠c. b−c always comes out in the form (t, −2t), a direction perpendicular to a. So you can move a vector by any amount in the direction perpendicular to a.
y-m-70-04.s.s3.prompt: You confirmed that the claim does not always hold. Choose all the following extra conditions that make 'if a·b=a·c then b=c' hold. (a is not the zero vector.)
y-m-70-04.s.s3.hint.0: Rewrite each condition as what kind of vector b−c must be. What does a·(b−c)=0 mean?
y-m-70-04.s.s3.hint.1: For each condition, directly look for a pair with b≠c when a=(2, 1). If you find one, that condition is not sufficient.
y-m-70-04.s.s3.o.a: |b|=|c| (the two vectors have the same size)
y-m-70-04.s.s3.r.a: Having the same size does not make them the same vector. Check whether b=(1, 3), c=(3, −1) satisfies the condition when a=(2, 1).
y-m-70-04.s.s3.o.b: a·b=a·c holds for every vector a in the plane
y-m-70-04.s.s3.r.b: This idea changes a while imposing the condition so that b−c is perpendicular to every direction.
y-m-70-04.s.s3.r.c: You missed that there are infinitely many vectors perpendicular to a on one line. For example, think of (1, −2) and (2, −4).
y-m-70-04.s.s3.o.d: b and c are both parallel to a
y-m-70-04.s.s3.r.d: This idea uses the fact that vectors on one line are fixed one by one by their size (the dot product).
y-m-70-04.s.s3.explain: Since a·(b−c)=0, it is enough for b−c to be perpendicular to a. (b) If it holds for every a, then b−c is perpendicular to every direction, so it is the zero vector. (d) If b=sa and c=ta, then s|a|²=t|a|² gives s=t. (a) If b=(1, 3), c=(3, −1), the sizes are equal and a·b=a·c=5, but b≠c. (c) (1, −2) and (2, −4) are both perpendicular to a so their dot product is 0, but they are different from each other.

y-m-70-05.title: If you cut a sphere with a plane, is the cross-section always a circle?
y-m-70-05.topic: Space coordinates: the equation of a sphere and its cross-section by the plane z=k
y-m-70-05.goal: Using the cross-section data given in a table as evidence, judge the claim 'the cross-section of a sphere is always a circle', find planes that give circles with integer radius, and explain how the size of the cross-section depends on position.
y-m-70-05.material:
The sphere S: (x−1)²+(y−2)²+(z−3)²=25 (center (1, 2, 3), radius 5) is cut by the plane z=k. Eunho said, “The cross-section of a sphere is always a circle,” and made the table below for several values of k. (k; all lengths are in the same unit)
k | equation of the intersection | shape of the cross-section
3 | (x−1)²+(y−2)²=25 | circle with center (1, 2, 3), radius 5
0 | (x−1)²+(y−2)²=16 | circle with center (1, 2, 0), radius 4
8 | (x−1)²+(y−2)²=0 | one point (1, 2, 8)
9 | (x−1)²+(y−2)²=−11 | no intersection points
y-m-70-05.thinking.0: Judging a generalization from evidence in a table
y-m-70-05.thinking.1: Finding several planes that satisfy a condition
y-m-70-05.thinking.2: Explaining using the symmetry of the sphere
y-m-70-05.prereq.0: Assume the learner is taking the high-school 'Geometry' elective course. 'H2' is only a difficulty and support level for this production assignment; it does not mean the Ministry of Education assigns this course to a particular grade.
y-m-70-05.prereq.2: Finding the intersection of the plane z=k and a sphere (substitute z=k into the equation)
y-m-70-05.s.s1.prompt: Judge Eunho's statement using the table as evidence.
y-m-70-05.s.s1.hint.0: Eunho's claim says 'always', so look in the table for even one row that is not a circle.
y-m-70-05.s.s1.hint.1: Think about what set of points you get when the right-hand side is 0 or negative, as for k=8 and 9.
y-m-70-05.s.s1.o.a: Correct. The rows k=3 and 0 are circles, so the cross-section of a sphere is always a circle
y-m-70-05.s.s1.r.a: This is a judgment that looked only at the cases that gave circles and ignored the rest.
y-m-70-05.s.s1.o.b: Wrong. Already at k=0 a cross-section that is not a circle appears
y-m-70-05.s.s1.r.b: The equation for k=0 is the equation of a circle of radius 4. Look again at what shape you get when the right-hand side of the equation is positive.
y-m-70-05.s.s1.o.c: It cannot be known from the table alone. There are also planes not of the form z=k
y-m-70-05.s.s1.r.c: If the cross-section is not a circle for even one plane of the form z=k, 'always' is broken. You missed that you do not need to check every plane to get a counterexample.
y-m-70-05.s.s1.o.d: Wrong. For k=8 and k=9 the cross-section is not a circle
y-m-70-05.s.s1.r.d: This is a judgment that uses the cases that break the generalization (a point and the empty set) as evidence.
y-m-70-05.s.s1.explain: The claim 'always a circle' is broken by one case that is not a circle. For k=8 it is one point and for k=9 there are no intersection points, so Eunho's statement does not hold. The planes of the form z=k alone give enough counterexamples.
y-m-70-05.s.s2.prompt: Write as pairs the values k and the radius r for which the cross-section by the plane z=k is a circle with natural-number radius (1, 2, 3, …). Make 3 examples with different k.
y-m-70-05.s.s2.hint.0: If the radius of the cross-section is r, the equation has the form (x−1)²+(y−2)²=r². Write how r² is expressed in terms of k when you substitute z=k.
y-m-70-05.s.s2.hint.1: Put in r = 1, 2, 3, 4, 5 one at a time and check whether (k−3)² is a perfect square.
y-m-70-05.s.s2.ok.c1: The radius is a natural number.
y-m-70-05.s.s2.fail.c1: The radius is not a natural number.
y-m-70-05.s.s2.ok.c2: The plane cuts the sphere in a circle of radius r.
y-m-70-05.s.s2.fail.c2: r²+(k−3)² is not 25. The radius of the cross-section is the square root of 25−(k−3)².
y-m-70-05.s.s2.explain: We need (k−3)²=25−r² with r a natural number. If r=5, then k=3; if r=4, then (k−3)²=9, so k=0 or 6; if r=3, then (k−3)²=16, so k=−1 or 7. For r=1 and 2, 25−1=24 and 25−4=21 are not perfect squares, so there is no integer k.
y-m-70-05.s.s3.prompt: Using the positions of the sphere's center and the planes, explain why k=0 and k=6 both give a circle of radius 4.
y-m-70-05.s.s3.hint.0: First write how far each of the two planes is from the center of the sphere (z-coordinate 3).
y-m-70-05.s.s3.hint.1: Recall what happens when you flip the sphere over the plane z=3.
y-m-70-05.s.s3.selfAssess.0: Does my explanation include 'the distance from the center to the two planes'?
y-m-70-05.s.s3.selfAssess.1: Did I check whether this reason also applies to k=−1 and 7, not just k=0 and 6?
y-m-70-05.s.s3.selfAssess.2: Does my explanation agree with the value calculated by the formula r²=25−(distance)²?
y-m-70-05.s.s3.model.0: The center of the sphere is at z=3, and k=0 and k=6 are each exactly 3 away from the center, one below and one above. The radius of the cross-section is the square root of 25 minus (distance)², so the cross-sections of the two planes are circles of the same size.
y-m-70-05.s.s3.model.1: The sphere is symmetric about the plane z=3 through its center, so the plane above and the plane below at the same distance from it make identical cross-sections. That is why k=0 and k=6 have the same radius 4.

y-m-70-06.title: The definition of a hyperbola, explained accurately to juniors
y-m-70-06.topic: Conic sections: the definition of a hyperbola (the difference of distances to the foci)
y-m-70-06.goal: Examine the conditions under which the set of points with a constant difference of distances is a hyperbola, find an inaccurate definition that is commonly used and correct it, and rewrite it as an accurate notice for juniors.
y-m-70-06.material: There are two pegs F(5, 0) and F′(−5, 0) with FF′=10 (unit cm). For a point P, we want to collect the points for which the absolute value of the difference of PF and PF′, |PF−PF′|, equals d, and draw a curve. Before writing a notice for the juniors in our club, let's first check what gets drawn depending on the value of d.
y-m-70-06.thinking.0: Testing the conditions of a definition
y-m-70-06.thinking.1: Finding the gaps in an inaccurate statement
y-m-70-06.thinking.2: Rewriting accurately with the reader in mind
y-m-70-06.prereq.0: Assume the learner is taking the high-school 'Geometry' elective course. 'H2' is only a difficulty and support level for this production assignment; it does not mean the Ministry of Education assigns this course to a particular grade.
y-m-70-06.prereq.1: The definition of a hyperbola (the absolute value of the difference of the distances to the two foci is constant)
y-m-70-06.prereq.2: In a triangle, the difference of two side lengths is not greater than the remaining side
y-m-70-06.s.s1.prompt: Choose all the values of d for which the set of points P satisfying |PF−PF′|=d is a hyperbola (with two branches).
y-m-70-06.s.s1.hint.0: Think about the fact that the distance between the pegs is 10 and estimate the largest value |PF−PF′| can take.
y-m-70-06.s.s1.hint.1: Mark a few points for d=0 and d=10 and say what figure they form.
y-m-70-06.s.s1.r.a: With |PF−PF′|=6, this is a value giving a hyperbola whose half major axis is 3.
y-m-70-06.s.s1.r.b: This is the set of points with PF=PF′. It becomes the line through the middle of the two pegs.
y-m-70-06.s.s1.r.c: This is a value greater than FF′=10. Think about whether such a point P can actually exist.
y-m-70-06.s.s1.r.d: This is the same value as FF′. Mark points directly to see what shape they form.
y-m-70-06.s.s1.r.e: With |PF−PF′|=4, this is a value giving a hyperbola whose half major axis is 2.
y-m-70-06.s.s1.explain: In triangle PFF′, |PF−PF′|≤FF′=10, so d cannot exceed 10. If d=0, then PF=PF′, so it is the line through the middle of the pegs (the y-axis). If d=10, it is the two rays on the line through the pegs, outside the pegs. It is a hyperbola only when 0<d<10; for d=6 it is x²/9−y²/16=1, and for d=4 it is x²/4−y²/21=1.
y-m-70-06.s.s2.prompt: A senior student wrote a draft of a notice to send to the juniors. Choose the one line that is not accurate.
y-m-70-06.s.s2.hint.0: Compare each line, one by one, with the range of d you confirmed in s1.
y-m-70-06.s.s2.hint.1: Trust line 2 first and compare it with line 1 to see whether line 1 alone gives both branches.
y-m-70-06.s.s2.line.0: A hyperbola is the set of points P for which the difference of distances PF−PF′ from the two points F(5, 0) and F′(−5, 0) is constant.
y-m-70-06.s.s2.line.1: If you collect only the points with PF−PF′=6, only the one branch nearer F′ appears.
y-m-70-06.s.s2.line.2: The difference of distances can be any number greater than 0, so a hyperbola is drawn even if you set d=12.
y-m-70-06.s.s2.line.3: If d=6, then 2a=6 gives a=3 and c=5, so b²=c²−a²=16.
y-m-70-06.s.s2.explain: Line 1 says only 'the difference PF−PF′', so it also includes points that give only one branch, and the definition is not complete (line 2 shows that fact). To be exact it is the absolute value of the difference. As you saw in s1, line 3 has no points if d=12. d must be greater than 0 and less than FF′. Line 4 is correct.
y-m-70-06.s.s3.prompt: Rewrite the notice for the juniors (2 to 3 sentences) so that the definition of a hyperbola is stated accurately. The gaps you found above must be fixed.
y-m-70-06.s.s3.hint.0: First mark what is inaccurate in line 1 and in line 3 of the draft.
y-m-70-06.s.s3.hint.1: Imagine a junior drawing it with string and pegs, and put in the 10 cm distance between the pegs and a value of d as an example.
y-m-70-06.s.s3.selfAssess.0: Does my writing contain both 'the absolute value of the difference' (or how the sign is handled) and the range of d?
y-m-70-06.s.s3.selfAssess.1: If a junior tries to draw with d=12 or d=10, does my writing help?
y-m-70-06.s.s3.selfAssess.2: Did I explain the difficult words at the juniors' level?
y-m-70-06.s.s3.model.0: When the two pegs F and F′ are 10 cm apart, marking and joining the points P for which the absolute value of the difference of distances to the two pegs is constant gives a hyperbola. The constant value must be greater than 0 and less than 10 cm. If the value is 10 you get rays on a line, and if it is 12 there are no points.
y-m-70-06.s.s3.model.1: A hyperbola is the set of points P with |PF−PF′|=d (0<d<10). When you subtract the two distances, subtract the smaller from the larger so it is always positive. Then the curve comes out in two branches, one on the F side and one on the F′ side.
y-m-70-06.s.s3.modelNote.1: An answer written briefly with symbols and equations

y-m-70-07.title: Adjusting the area made by a point inside a triangle with coefficients
y-m-70-07.topic: Plane vectors: the linear combination AP=sAB+tAC and the area of a triangle
y-m-70-07.goal: Discover for yourself the relationship between the coefficients of a point written as a linear combination of vectors and the areas of triangles, make several points that satisfy an area condition, and explain why two area conditions fix a single point.
y-m-70-07.material: There is a triangle ABC (the three points are not on one line), and a point P is written as AP = s·AB + t·AC. (AP, AB and AC are vectors, and s and t are real numbers. Read it as 'vector AP equals s times vector AB plus t times vector AC'.) Consider the case where point P is inside triangle ABC.
y-m-70-07.thinking.0: Discovering the relationship between coefficients and geometric quantities
y-m-70-07.thinking.1: Constructing several points that satisfy a condition
y-m-70-07.thinking.2: Reasoning about how many solutions there are as conditions are added
y-m-70-07.prereq.0: Assume the learner is taking the high-school 'Geometry' elective course. 'H2' is only a difficulty and support level for this production assignment; it does not mean the Ministry of Education assigns this course to a particular grade.
y-m-70-07.prereq.1: Linear combinations of plane vectors (AP=sAB+tAC) and the size and direction of vectors
y-m-70-07.prereq.2: The area of a triangle is half the product of the base and the height
y-m-70-07.s.s1.prompt: Which one decides how many times the area of triangle PAB is the area of triangle ABC?
y-m-70-07.s.s1.hint.0: Compare the height from P to line AB with the height from C to line AB.
y-m-70-07.s.s1.hint.1: Say where P is when s=0 and when t=0.
y-m-70-07.s.s1.explain: In P=A+s·AB+t·AC, moving by s in the direction of AB does not change the height to line AB, and moving by t in the direction of AC makes the height t times the height of C. Since the base AB is the same, (area of triangle PAB) : (area of triangle ABC)=t : 1. For the same reason PAC is s times and PBC is 1−s−t times.
y-m-70-07.s.s2.prompt: Make 3 pairs (s, t), with different s, such that the area of triangle PAB is 1/4 of the area of triangle ABC. (P must be inside triangle ABC.)
y-m-70-07.s.s2.hint.0: First decide the coefficient you found in the previous step that determines the ratio of the areas.
y-m-70-07.s.s2.hint.1: Compare the range in which the remaining coefficient is free with the condition for P to be inside.
y-m-70-07.s.s2.fail.c1: For P to be inside, s>0, t>0 and s+t<1 are needed.
y-m-70-07.s.s2.ok.c2: The area of triangle PAB is 1/4 of ABC.
y-m-70-07.s.s2.fail.c2: The area of triangle PAB is not 1/4 of ABC. Check again which coefficient determines the ratio of the areas.
y-m-70-07.s.s2.explain: t=1/4 is fixed and s can be any value with 0<s<3/4 (s+t<1). So there are infinitely many solutions. These points are the points on the segment parallel to side AB at 1/4 of the height from AB.
y-m-70-07.s.s3.prompt: This time we want to find the point P such that the area of triangle PAB is 1/4 of ABC and at the same time the area of triangle PAC is 1/3 of ABC. How many such (s, t) are there, and what are they? Write the reason too.
y-m-70-07.s.s3.hint.1: Put the s and t found that way into s+t<1 and check whether P is inside.
y-m-70-07.s.s3.selfAssess.0: Are the values of s and t I wrote swapped relative to PAC=1/3 and PAB=1/4?
y-m-70-07.s.s3.selfAssess.1: Did I check s+t<1 to show that P is inside?
y-m-70-07.s.s3.selfAssess.2: Did I explain why there is only one point by saying the two conditions fix both coefficients?
y-m-70-07.s.s3.model.0: The area of PAC is decided by s and the area of PAB by t, so s=1/3 and t=1/4; both values are fixed, so there is only one point. s+t=7/12<1, so P is inside the triangle.
y-m-70-07.s.s3.model.1: The ratio of the areas equals t for PAB and s for PAC. So only (s, t)=(1/3, 1/4) is possible. The sum is 7/12, less than 1, so it is a point inside.
y-m-70-07.s.s3.modelNote.1: An answer that includes checking that the point is inside

y-m-70-08.title: The shadow of a tilted panel: what rule does its area follow?
y-m-70-08.topic: Solids in space: the area of an orthogonal projection and the dihedral angle
y-m-70-08.goal: Sift through several candidate rules one by one with measurement data and adjust your confidence, and explain with a rectangle why the area of an orthogonal projection is cosθ times the original.
y-m-70-08.material: There is a square solar panel with side length 6 m. It is placed with one side parallel to the ground (horizontal), and the panel is tilted about that side as the axis; call the angle it makes with the ground θ. Assuming simply that sunlight falls perpendicular to the ground, we look one at a time at data measuring the area S(θ) of the shadow (orthogonal projection) on the ground. There are three candidate rules. (가) S=36·cosθ, (나) S=36·(1−θ/90°), (다) S=36·cos²θ. (cos is read 'cosine', and cos²θ is read 'cosine theta squared'.)
y-m-70-08.thinking.1: Adjusting confidence according to new data
y-m-70-08.thinking.2: Explaining the reason for the general rule
y-m-70-08.prereq.0: Assume the learner is taking the high-school 'Geometry' elective course. 'H2' is only a difficulty and support level for this production assignment; it does not mean the Ministry of Education assigns this course to a particular grade.
y-m-70-08.prereq.1: The meaning of the angle between two planes (dihedral angle)
y-m-70-08.prereq.2: The trigonometric ratio cosθ and its values at special angles (0°, 45°, 60°, 90°)
y-m-70-08.s.s1.prompt: Looking at the data one step at a time, choose your current judgment about the three candidates.
y-m-70-08.s.s1.hint.0: Compare in a table the value you get by putting θ into each candidate with the measured value.
y-m-70-08.s.s1.hint.1: Tell apart the θ for which the three candidates give the same value from the θ for which they give different values.
y-m-70-08.s.s1.st.0.info: At θ=0° (lying flat), S=36 m² was measured, and at θ=90° (standing up), S=0 m².
y-m-70-08.s.s1.st.0.ask: What is your current judgment about the three candidates?
y-m-70-08.s.s1.st.0.after: All three candidates give 36 at θ=0° and 0 at θ=90°, so this data alone cannot separate them. Leaning toward the rule you know first can be taken as a hypothesis, but the evidence is still weak.
y-m-70-08.s.s1.st.0.o.a: I think (가) is likely right, but the evidence is still weak
y-m-70-08.s.s1.st.0.r.a: You are leaning toward the rule you know first. Work out whether this data alone eliminates the other candidates.
y-m-70-08.s.s1.st.0.o.b: All three candidates agree with this data, so they cannot be separated yet
y-m-70-08.s.s1.st.0.r.b: This is a judgment made after checking that putting θ=0° and 90° into all three candidates gives 36 and 0.
y-m-70-08.s.s1.st.0.o.c: (나) is right. It is natural for the area to decrease as much as the angle increases
y-m-70-08.s.s1.st.0.r.c: This judgment comes from the thought 'it is proportional, so it is the simplest'.
y-m-70-08.s.s1.st.0.o.d: (다) is right. Because the shape that ends at 0 is a square
y-m-70-08.s.s1.st.0.r.d: This is a judgment made by looking only at the shape of the formula, regardless of the data.
y-m-70-08.s.s1.st.1.info: At θ=60°, S=18 m² was measured.
y-m-70-08.s.s1.st.1.ask: The values of the three candidates are (가) 36·cos60°, (나) 36·(1−60/90), (다) 36·cos²60°. What is your judgment after seeing this data?
y-m-70-08.s.s1.st.1.after: 36·cos60°=36·(1/2)=18, 36·(1−2/3)=12, 36·(1/4)=9. Only candidate (가) matches the measured value 18.
y-m-70-08.s.s1.st.1.o.a: (나) remains. Its value is closest to 12
y-m-70-08.s.s1.st.1.r.a: The value of (나) is 12. It is far from the measured 18.
y-m-70-08.s.s1.st.1.o.b: (다) remains. It is not strange that the value comes out small, 9
y-m-70-08.s.s1.st.1.r.b: The value of (다) is 9, half of the measured 18.
y-m-70-08.s.s1.st.1.r.c: This is a judgment made by comparing the values from putting θ=60° into the three candidates with the measured value.
y-m-70-08.s.s1.st.2.info: At θ=45°, S was measured as about 25.5 m² (measurement error ±0.3 m²).
y-m-70-08.s.s1.st.2.ask: The prediction of (가) is 36·cos45°≈25.46. How does this data change your confidence in (가)?
y-m-70-08.s.s1.st.2.after: The prediction 25.46 of (가) agrees with the measured 25.5 within the error range, and differs greatly from the prediction 18 of (나) and (다). It is reasonable to say your confidence went up, or to say it was already sufficient.
y-m-70-08.s.s1.st.2.o.a: It went down. Because 25.5 is not exactly 25.46
y-m-70-08.s.s1.st.2.r.a: You ignored the condition that the measurement has error. Look at whether it falls within the error range.
y-m-70-08.s.s1.st.2.o.b: It went up. The prediction is right within the error range and the prediction 18 of (나) and (다) is far off
y-m-70-08.s.s1.st.2.r.b: This is a judgment that the new data agrees with the prediction of (가), so confidence rose.
y-m-70-08.s.s1.st.2.o.c: It did not change. (나) and (다) were already eliminated at 60°, and 45° does not contradict (가) either
y-m-70-08.s.s1.st.2.r.c: This is a judgment that the new data does not contradict the judgment already made.
y-m-70-08.s.s1.reflect: With the first data the candidates could not be separated, with the second data the candidates were sifted out, and the third data did not change the judgment but only raised confidence. Say which data changed your judgment the most and why.
y-m-70-08.s.s2.prompt: Does rule (가) also hold for a rectangular panel instead of a square one? When a rectangular panel with width a (parallel to the tilting axis) and length b is tilted in the same way, write how many times the width, the length and the area of the shadow are the originals, with the reasons.
y-m-70-08.s.s2.hint.0: Work out what happens to the lengths of the side parallel to the tilting axis and the side perpendicular to it when they are cast on the ground.
y-m-70-08.s.s2.hint.1: First check the width and length of the shadow at θ=0° and θ=90°.
y-m-70-08.s.s2.selfAssess.0: Did I write the width and the length of the shadow separately?
y-m-70-08.s.s2.selfAssess.1: Did I tell apart the direction that stays 'the same' from the direction that 'shrinks'?
y-m-70-08.s.s2.selfAssess.2: Did I test whether my formula is right at θ=0° and 90°?
y-m-70-08.s.s2.model.0: The width side parallel to the tilting axis stays a in the shadow too, and the length side perpendicular to it shrinks to b·cosθ. The shadow is a rectangle with width a and length b·cosθ, so its area is ab·cosθ, which is cosθ times the original area.
y-m-70-08.s.s2.model.1: The width does not change and the length in one direction becomes cosθ times, so the area is also cosθ times. It is 1 times at θ=0° and 0 times at θ=90°, which agrees with the data too.
y-m-70-08.s.s2.modelNote.1: An answer checked with extreme values

y-m-70-09.title: If a line meets a parabola at one point, is it a tangent?
y-m-70-09.topic: Conic sections: positions of a parabola and a line, tangent lines
y-m-70-09.goal: Judge the claim 'if it meets at one point, it is a tangent' using evidence in a table and look for a counterexample, build pairs (m, n) that give tangent lines of a parabola yourself, and explain the case that the discriminant cannot distinguish.
y-m-70-09.thinking.0: Judging a claim with evidence in a table
y-m-70-09.thinking.1: Setting up the tangent condition and building several examples
y-m-70-09.thinking.2: Explaining the limits of a method
y-m-70-09.prereq.0: Assume the learner is taking the high-school 'Geometry' elective course. 'H2' is only a difficulty and support level for this production assignment; it does not mean the Ministry of Education assigns this course to a particular grade.
y-m-70-09.prereq.1: The tangent y₁y=2(x+x₁) at a point (x₁, y₁) on the parabola y²=4x
y-m-70-09.prereq.2: The discriminant of a quadratic equation
y-m-70-09.s.s1.prompt: Judge Jisu's statement using the table and the note as evidence.
y-m-70-09.s.s1.o.a: Correct. In the table, the lines that meet at one point (m=0, m=1) are all tangents
y-m-70-09.s.s1.r.a: You did not check whether the line for m=0 is the same as the tangent at (1/4, 1).
y-m-70-09.s.s1.o.d: Wrong. A tangent always meets the parabola at two points
y-m-70-09.s.s1.r.d: This judgment differs from the definition that a tangent touches at one point.
y-m-70-09.s.s1.explain: The line y=1 with m=0 meets C at one point (1/4, 1), but the tangent at that point is y=2x+1/2, so it differs from y=1. The line y=1 is parallel to the axis (the x-axis) of the parabola, so even though it meets at one point, it is not a tangent. One counterexample makes Jisu's statement false. On the other hand, m=1 is the same as the tangent y=x+1, so it is a tangent.
y-m-70-09.s.s2.prompt: Make 3 pairs (m, n), with different m, for which the line y=mx+n is a tangent to the parabola y²=4x. (Exclude lines parallel to the axis and those of the form x=k. You may use decimals.)
y-m-70-09.s.s2.hint.0: Substitute y=mx+n into y²=4x and make an expression in x. Is it quadratic?
y-m-70-09.s.s2.hint.1: Think about what state of this equation's solutions being tangent corresponds to, and set up an equation using the discriminant.
y-m-70-09.s.s2.fail.c1: If m=0, the line is parallel to the axis of the parabola, so it is not a tangent.
y-m-70-09.s.s2.ok.c2: The line y=mx+n is tangent to y²=4x.
y-m-70-09.s.s2.fail.c2: Substitute y=mx+n into y²=4x to make a quadratic equation in x, and check the condition for it to have a double root.
y-m-70-09.s.s2.explain: Rearranging (mx+n)²=4x gives m²x²+(2mn−4)x+n²=0, and from the discriminant (2mn−4)²−4m²n²=16−16mn=0 we get mn=1. That is, y=mx+1/m (m≠0) is a tangent. Examples: (1, 1), (2, 1/2), (−1, −1). x=0 (the y-axis) is not of the form y=mx+n, but it is the tangent at the vertex.
y-m-70-09.s.s3.prompt: For a line like y=1 that meets the parabola at one point but is not a tangent, how does it go against the method of checking the tangent condition with the discriminant after substitution? Explain briefly.
y-m-70-09.s.s3.hint.0: Look at what degree the substituted expression −4x+1=0 is when m=0.
y-m-70-09.s.s3.hint.1: Compare what degree an expression must be for the discriminant to be able to speak of a 'double root'.
y-m-70-09.s.s3.selfAssess.0: Did I say that for m=0 it is a linear expression, not a quadratic one?
y-m-70-09.s.s3.selfAssess.1: Did I tell 'meets at one point' and 'is tangent' apart?
y-m-70-09.s.s3.selfAssess.2: Did I think about why a line parallel to the axis is special only for a parabola?
y-m-70-09.s.s3.model.0: When m=0, the substituted expression is linear and has only one solution. In this case you cannot use the discriminant to look for a double root, and this line is parallel to the axis, so even though it meets at one point it is not a tangent.
y-m-70-09.s.s3.model.1: A discriminant of 0 means that a quadratic equation has a double root, so the line is tangent. A line parallel to the axis gives a linear expression, so the discriminant condition does not apply, yet it meets at one point. So meeting at one point does not make it a tangent.
y-m-70-09.s.s3.modelNote.1: An answer stating the premise of the discriminant

y-m-70-10.title: If a line is perpendicular to two different lines in a plane, is it perpendicular to the plane?
y-m-70-10.topic: Solids in space: perpendicularity of a line and a plane (expressed with direction vectors)
y-m-70-10.goal: Find the missing condition in the claim 'if a line is perpendicular to two different lines in a plane, it is perpendicular to the plane', build a counterexample yourself using coordinates, and explain why that condition is needed.
y-m-70-10.material: In space coordinates the plane α is z=0 (the xy-plane). Let the direction vector of line l be d=(a, b, c) (not the zero vector), and let us agree that two lines being perpendicular means the dot product of their direction vectors is 0 (we decide by direction even if they do not meet). A student said, “If a line l is perpendicular to each of two different lines m₁ and m₂ in the plane α, then l is perpendicular to α.” The direction vector of m₁ is (1, 0, 0).
y-m-70-10.thinking.0: Pointing out the condition missing from the claim
y-m-70-10.thinking.2: Explaining why the needed condition is needed
y-m-70-10.prereq.0: Assume the learner is taking the high-school 'Geometry' elective course. 'H2' is only a difficulty and support level for this production assignment; it does not mean the Ministry of Education assigns this course to a particular grade.
y-m-70-10.prereq.1: Space coordinates and the direction vector (components) of a line
y-m-70-10.prereq.2: If two vectors are perpendicular, their dot product is 0
y-m-70-10.prereq.3: Two different lines through a point in a plane determine the plane
y-m-70-10.s.s1.prompt: For this statement to always hold, what more is needed about m₁ and m₂?
y-m-70-10.s.s1.hint.0: Write what the direction vectors are when m₁ and m₂ are parallel to each other.
y-m-70-10.s.s1.hint.1: Test with specific direction vectors whether there is a situation in which l being perpendicular to just one direction is enough.
y-m-70-10.s.s1.o.a: l passes through a point of α
y-m-70-10.s.s1.r.a: l meeting α does not make it perpendicular. A slanted line also meets at one point.
y-m-70-10.s.s1.o.b: One of m₁ and m₂ passes through the origin
y-m-70-10.s.s1.r.b: Which point a line passes through has nothing to do with its direction vector. Just changing the position gives the same direction.
y-m-70-10.s.s1.o.c: m₁ and m₂ are not parallel to each other
y-m-70-10.s.s1.r.c: This idea examined whether the perpendicularity condition covers two different directions in the plane.
y-m-70-10.s.s1.o.d: The z-component c of the direction vector of l is not 0
y-m-70-10.s.s1.r.d: Even if the z-component is not 0, l may not be perpendicular to α. Think of (0, 1, 1).
y-m-70-10.s.s1.explain: If m₁ and m₂ are parallel, there is only one direction, so it is enough for l to be perpendicular to one direction. So a slanted line can also be perpendicular to both lines. If the two lines are not parallel, l is perpendicular to two different directions in the plane, so it is perpendicular to every direction of the plane.
y-m-70-10.s.s2.prompt: When the direction vector of m₁ is (1, 0, 0) and that of m₂ is (−2, 0, 0) (parallel to each other), make 3 direction vectors (a, b, c), in different directions, of lines l that are perpendicular to both m₁ and m₂ but not perpendicular to α. (If l is perpendicular to α, the direction vector has the form (0, 0, c).)
y-m-70-10.s.s2.hint.0: Calculate each dot product and first decide the condition on a.
y-m-70-10.s.s2.hint.1: Compare with the perpendicular form (0, 0, c) and find what condition on b makes it not perpendicular.
y-m-70-10.s.s2.ok.c1: l is perpendicular to both m₁ and m₂.
y-m-70-10.s.s2.fail.c1: The dot products of (a, b, c) with (1, 0, 0) and (−2, 0, 0) are not 0. Calculate the dot products.
y-m-70-10.s.s2.ok.c2: l is not perpendicular to α.
y-m-70-10.s.s2.fail.c2: If the direction vector has the form (0, 0, c), l is perpendicular to α. b must not be 0 for it not to be perpendicular.
y-m-70-10.s.s2.explain: The dot product of (1, 0, 0) and (a, b, c) is a, and with (−2, 0, 0) it is −2a, so if both are 0 then a=0. But for (0, b, c) to be perpendicular to α we need b=0, so if b≠0 it is not perpendicular. Example: (0, 1, 1) is perpendicular to both lines but not perpendicular to α.
y-m-70-10.s.s3.prompt: Using the examples you made above, write a note to a friend explaining why the condition 'not parallel' is really needed in this theorem.
y-m-70-10.s.s3.hint.0: Compare how many directions two parallel lines give and how many directions of the plane α are needed.
y-m-70-10.s.s3.hint.1: Explain using one of your examples (for example (0, 1, 1)).
y-m-70-10.s.s3.selfAssess.0: Does my writing include the reason 'if they are parallel there is only one direction'?
y-m-70-10.s.s3.selfAssess.1: Did I use the direction vectors I made as evidence?
y-m-70-10.s.s3.selfAssess.2: Did I add a word on 'why not parallel is enough'?
y-m-70-10.s.s3.model.0: If m₁ and m₂ are parallel, there is only one direction, so l only needs to be perpendicular to that one direction. For example, if the direction of l is (0, 1, 1), it is perpendicular to both lines but not perpendicular to α. So the two lines must be non-parallel.
y-m-70-10.s.s3.model.1: A plane is determined only when it has two different directions, but two parallel lines actually give only one direction. Even if l is tilted it can be perpendicular to that direction, so a counterexample arises.
